title: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Network systems whose rewiring rules depend only on whether a node's two connections lead to the same node always grow in an essentially repetitive way, but when rules depend on nodes up to two connections away, even the number of nodes can vary in an apparently random way (in about one in 10,000 rules).

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: even the total number of nodes at each step can vary in a way that seems in many respects completely random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Network Systems” (from p. 193), p. 201. Scope: network systems with local rewiring and node-insertion rules

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The systems are finite-description programs and their claimed prevalence can be directly estimated or enumerated. Existing computation can resolve bounded horizons and frequencies, but not prove unrestricted randomness for all qualifying trajectories.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate the stated local rewiring-rule classes, run each from standardized initial networks, and classify node-count series for repetition, nesting, and statistical irregularity. Estimate the fraction of distance-two rules meeting preregistered randomness criteria and test the restricted-class repetition assertion.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Apparent randomness is test-dependent.

Long transients can masquerade as nonrepetition.

The exact rule grammar and equivalence classes affect the one-in-10,000 frequency.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.82
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.72
data adequacy: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The two rule families are described precisely enough to resample, and public graph libraries can apply the rewrites. A sample large enough to estimate a one-in-ten-thousand rate, with long enough evolutions to trust the irregular cases, is a specialist project of weeks to months rather than a routine analysis. The qualitative contrast, repetitive at distance one and sometimes irregular at distance two, is the part that existing computation can actually pin down.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate network rewiring rules that branch on whether the two outgoing edges meet, and then rules that branch on the number of distinct nodes within distance two, and record the node-count series. Universal eventual repetition in the first family, and an irregular fraction on the order of 1 in 10,000 in the second, would support the claim; a much higher irregular fraction, or a short period in the alleged random examples, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A node count can look random for a long time and then fall into a long cycle, and growing networks make those runs expensive.

The rate 'about one in 10,000' depends on the encoding and the measure used to draw random rules.
